opus-5.5.text:
I think the crucial test over the next five years is whether we can move from impressive demos to robots that actually create value in real, open environments — at scale, every day, without a team of engineers standing behind them.

Right now the industry has a lot of excitement. You see videos of humanoids folding clothes, dancing, doing backflips. But a demo is one success out of maybe many tries, in a controlled setting. The real question is generalization: can a robot walk into a home or a store it has never seen, deal with objects it has never touched, and still complete the task reliably? That's the dividing line between a research prototype and a product.

And underneath that is the data problem. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Embodied intelligence doesn't have an internet of robot actions. So the test is really whether we can find a scalable data pipeline — whether through large-scale synthetic data and simulation, through teleoperation, through learning from human video, or some combination — that lets capability grow the way it did for large models. In my own view, simulation and synthetic data have to carry a big share of that load, because real-world data collection alone is too slow and too expensive to reach the scale we need.

Then there's the commercial side. Within five years, I think the industry has to show a closed loop: robots deployed in some real scenario — maybe retail, logistics, factories, pharmacies — doing useful work, generating revenue, and also generating data that feeds back into making the model better. If that flywheel starts turning, the field takes off. If it doesn't, and we're still mostly showing demos and raising money on expectations, there will be a serious correction.

So to put it simply: the test is whether embodied intelligence can prove real generalization and real value, rather than just looking intelligent on video.

r001.rationale: The response describes proving real-world value and deployment within five years, but gives no annual deployment target of 10,000 autonomous robots.

r002.rationale: It warns of a serious correction if the industry remains focused on demos and expectations, but does not say that failing to reach 10,000 annual deployments could leave revenue far below promises, like industrial vision.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the crucial test is whether we can actually close the data loop, and I mean that in a very concrete way.

Right now the whole field is riding on an analogy to large language models: scale up data, scale up the model, and intelligence emerges. The analogy is seductive, and I believe in it directionally. But language had the internet. Decades of humans writing text for free, trillions of tokens sitting there waiting to be scraped. Robots have nothing like that. There is no internet of manipulation data. Every trajectory of a hand grasping a cup, folding a towel, inserting a connector, somebody had to generate it, either through teleoperation at considerable cost, or in simulation with all the sim-to-real problems that come with it.

So the question for the next five years is not "can we build a big model." We can. The question is whether we can establish a flywheel where robots deployed in the real world generate useful data, that data makes the next model better, and the better model makes deployment economically viable at a larger scale, which generates more data. If that loop closes, this becomes an industry. If it doesn't, we have a very impressive research field with beautiful demo videos and no business.

And I want to be honest about where I think the risk is. The hard part of that loop is the first deployment. You need a model that is good enough to be useful for a real customer, in a real factory or warehouse or home, with reliability that is not ninety percent but closer to ninety-nine point something. Ninety percent success looks wonderful on a conference stage and is useless on a production line. That gap, from the demo to the deployment threshold, is where I think most of the industry's effort and most of its casualties will be over the next five years.

My own view on how you get across that gap is that you cannot rely on real-world teleoperation alone. The cost per trajectory is too high, and the diversity is too low. You need simulation and synthetic data to carry the long tail, and you need to actually solve the generalization problem, not paper over it with more demonstrations of the same scene. That is why I keep coming back to generalizable manipulation, dexterous hands, learning from diverse geometry rather than memorizing specific objects. If the model only works on the objects it has seen, then you are back to collecting data for every new customer, and the loop never closes.

The second part of the test is about hardware, and this one is a bit uncomfortable to say out loud. A lot of what we are learning about intelligence right now is being learned on hardware that is not reliable enough. Dexterous hands break. Actuators have inconsistent response. If you cannot run a robot for ten thousand hours without maintenance, you cannot collect ten thousand hours of data from it, and you cannot sell it to anyone either. So part of the test over five years is whether the hardware supply chain matures to the point where the robot itself stops being the bottleneck. I actually think China is in a strong position here, because of the manufacturing ecosystem, but the industry needs to resist the temptation to ship a beautiful humanoid that works for twenty minutes.

If I had to compress all of that into one sentence: the test is whether, five years from now, there exist robots doing real work for paying customers in a way that produces data nobody had to pay for separately. If yes, this is the beginning of something as big as everyone claims. If no, we will be having this same conversation about when the flywheel is going to start.

r001.rationale: The response describes real-world deployment as the test but does not specify annual deployment of at least 10,000 autonomous robots within five years.

r002.rationale: It warns that the field could remain research with no business if the data loop fails, but does not mention the 10,000-robot annual threshold or compare the outcome to industrial vision’s revenue falling short of initial promises.

astra-6.text:
I think the crucial test is whether embodied intelligence can move from impressive demonstrations to dependable work in real environments. Can a robot handle situations it hasn’t seen before, recover when something goes wrong, and keep operating without someone constantly stepping in?

Over the next five years, I would look for sustained deployment: robots doing useful tasks day after day, at a cost that makes sense for the people using them. A successful demonstration is a starting point. The harder test is whether customers continue using the system because it reliably solves a problem.

That also tests how broadly the technology can generalize. If every new task or environment requires extensive custom engineering, deployment will remain difficult to scale. The real breakthrough would be robots that can learn new tasks and adapt to new settings with substantially less effort.

r001.rationale: The response describes sustained, dependable robot deployment but does not identify annual deployment of at least 10,000 autonomous robots by leading companies as the five-year test.

r002.rationale: The response does not warn that missing the 10,000 annual deployment target could leave the industry resembling industrial vision or producing revenue far below initial promises.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the crucial test is whether embodied intelligence can move from impressive demonstrations to reliable work in real environments. Can a robot handle unfamiliar objects, recover when something goes wrong, and keep working without an engineer standing beside it?

Over the next five years, we need to see that reliability translate into economic value. A customer has to be able to say: this robot performs a useful task, the cost makes sense, and I want to deploy more of them. That includes the cost of maintenance and human intervention, not just the purchase price.

So I would watch repeat deployments more closely than demonstration videos. If customers keep buying and using these systems because they solve real problems, that will be strong evidence that the industry is moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses repeat deployments but does not specify 10,000 autonomous robots per year or identify that threshold as the five-year test.

r002.rationale: It does not warn about falling short of 10,000 annual deployments or compare the outcome to industrial vision and its revenue falling short of promises.
